items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A second-grade teacher is demonstrating how to read the word "cupcake" by thinking aloud about syllable types. Which explanation best applies that knowledge?
choices: "The first part ends in a consonant, so that vowel is likely short; the second part has a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so that vowel is likely long. I'll try cup-cake."
"Both parts end in a consonant, so both vowels are short. I'll say cup-cak."
"I'll say the sound for each letter and push them together."
"Both parts have two vowels together, so I'll use the long sound in each one."
items.correct_answer: "The first part ends in a consonant, so that vowel is likely short; the second part has a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so that vowel is likely long. I'll try cup-cake."
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how syllable-type knowledge is explained to students. The teacher names the two different syllable types in the word, states the vowel expectation each one carries, and then uses those expectations to generate a pronunciation, which is exactly the reasoning students need to hear modeled before they can do it themselves.

distractor_explanations.\"Both parts end in a consonant, so both: Applying the closed-syllable expectation to a vowel-consonant-e syllable The second syllable is not closed; it ends in a vowel-consonant-e pattern, so applying the closed-syllable expectation to it produces a nonword. This explanation overgeneralizes one syllable type across a word that contains two different ones.
distractor_explanations.\"I'll say the sound for each letter and: Substituting letter-by-letter blending for the syllable-level analysis longer words require Saying each letter sound and blending may work for short single-syllable words, but it gives students nothing to use on longer words. A demonstration of syllable types should show the larger unit of analysis, not retreat to letter-by-letter blending.
distractor_explanations.\"Both parts have two vowels together, s: Misreading a syllable's internal structure and treating it as a vowel team Neither syllable contains a vowel team. Describing the word this way misreads its structure and sends students to the wrong rule for the wrong reason.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Ms. Ochoa is writing a small-group lesson whose objective is phoneme substitution. She sketches four possible tasks. Which example best supports that objective?
choices: Students sort picture cards by whether the name of the picture begins with /m/
Students say mat, are told to change /m/ to /s/, and say the new word
Students blend the sounds /s/ /a/ /t/ to say sat
Students clap the three syllables in Saturday
items.correct_answer: Students say mat, are told to change /m/ to /s/, and say the new word
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to evaluate an example against a specific instructional goal. Substitution is a manipulation task: the student holds the word in memory, removes one phoneme, inserts another, and produces the result. Turning mat into sat does exactly that, at the phoneme level and at the right level of difficulty for the stated objective.

distractor_explanations.Students sort picture cards by whether t: Treats isolating and sorting initial sounds as manipulation, when recognizing a phoneme is only the prerequisite for changing one and hearing what the change produces. Sorting by initial sound asks students to isolate and compare one phoneme across words. That is a beginning-level identification task; it does not require changing a word and hearing what the change produces.
distractor_explanations.Students blend the sounds /s/ /a/ /t/ to: Accepts blending as substitution, though blending only combines sounds while substitution also requires holding the word in memory, removing one, and inserting another. Blending asks students to combine sounds into a word. It is a prerequisite for substitution rather than the same operation, because nothing is removed or replaced.
distractor_explanations.Students clap the three syllables in Sat: Overlooks that syllables are far larger units than phonemes, so a clapping task never reaches the level the objective names. Clapping the syllables in Saturday works at the syllable level, far above the individual phoneme, and the operation is segmentation rather than substitution.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A teacher is planning word-analysis instruction and wants the end-of-year target to match grade-level expectations. Which decoding task is most appropriate for students at the end of first grade?
choices: Using morphological analysis to unlock the meaning of words such as "unhappy" and "replay"
Using context to confirm the pronunciation of multisyllabic content words such as "habitat"
Blending three phonemes to read single-syllable words such as "cat" and "mop"
Decoding two-syllable words with common long-vowel patterns such as "paper" and "reptile"
items.correct_answer: Decoding two-syllable words with common long-vowel patterns such as "paper" and "reptile"
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word-analysis expectations shift by grade. By the end of first grade, students are expected to apply their letter-sound knowledge to two-syllable words that follow regular patterns, dividing the word into syllables and reading each part before blending them into a known word.

distractor_explanations.Using morphological analysis to unlock t: Introducing morphological analysis before students can reliably decode single- and two-syllable words Morphological analysis of prefixes and suffixes is normally introduced after students reliably decode single- and two-syllable words. Asking first graders to use it as a primary decoding route sets the task well above their current word-analysis repertoire.
distractor_explanations.Using context to confirm the pronunciati: Using context to generate a pronunciation as a substitute for letter-sound analysis Checking a decoded word against context is a useful verification step, but it is not itself a decoding procedure. Using context to generate pronunciation bypasses the letter-sound analysis students need to develop.
distractor_explanations.Blending three phonemes to read single-s: Treating beginning-of-year CVC blending as an appropriate end-of-first-grade decoding target Blending three phonemes in CVC words is an early-first-grade target, not an exit target. Choosing it holds students below grade level and leaves them without the syllable-level strategies the later grades assume.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A first-grade student writes "kik" for "kick." The teacher notes that every letter the student used represents a plausible sound. Which response best builds the student's understanding of spelling conventions?
choices: Having the student practice forming the letters k, i, and c correctly
Telling the student the correct spelling and having the student copy it five times
Deferring any discussion of the spelling until the student reads more fluently
Explaining that the /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word after a short vowel is usually spelled ck, and having the student sort words by their final /k/ spelling
items.correct_answer: Explaining that the /k/ sound at the end of a one-syllable word after a short vowel is usually spelled ck, and having the student sort words by their final /k/ spelling
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how conventional spellings are taught. The student's attempt is phonetically defensible, so the next move is to make the convention explicit and give the student a set of examples that reveals when the language uses k and when it uses ck. Sorting turns a one-off correction into a generalizable pattern.

distractor_explanations.Having the student practice forming the: Attributing a spelling error to letter formation rather than to an unlearned spelling convention The student's letters are legible and correctly formed; the issue is which letter represents the final sound, not how the letters are written. Handwriting practice would leave the actual error untouched.
distractor_explanations.Telling the student the correct spelling: Equating repeated copying of a corrected word with instruction in a spelling generalization Copying a correct model may fix this one word for this one day, but it does not tell the student why ck is used here. Without attention to the pattern, the same error reappears with "back," "pick," and "duck."
distractor_explanations.Deferring any discussion of the spelling: Assuming instruction in spelling conventions should wait until fluency improves Encoding and decoding develop together, and instruction in one supports the other. Waiting for fluency to improve first delays the spelling knowledge that would support both.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A kindergarten teacher wants to build students' expressive language during a unit on plants. Which routine would best accomplish this goal?
choices: Giving students a page of plant words to trace and copy
Asking students to listen quietly while the teacher reads a book about how seeds travel
Having partners take turns telling how their own seedling changed, using the frame "First ___, then ___, and now ___"
Showing students labeled photos of roots, stems, and leaves and asking them to point to the stem
items.correct_answer: Having partners take turns telling how their own seedling changed, using the frame "First ___, then ___, and now ___"
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how expressive language is developed. Expressive language grows only when students produce extended oral output themselves. The sentence frame lowers the planning load so students can spend their effort on putting a real observation into words, and the partner format guarantees every student a turn instead of only the volunteers who already speak readily.

distractor_explanations.Giving students a page of plant words to: Assuming that tracing and copying words builds spoken language Option (D) is incorrect. Tracing and copying are print and handwriting tasks. They produce marks on a page rather than spoken language, so they leave the expressive channel unexercised.
distractor_explanations.Asking students to listen quietly while: Equating rich receptive input with the development of expressive output Option (A) is incorrect. A read-aloud supplies rich vocabulary and sentence structures, but it asks students to receive language, not to generate it. Rich input is a necessary companion to expressive work, not a substitute for it.
distractor_explanations.Showing students labeled photos of roots: Treating pointing and recognition responses as if they forced students to generate language Option (C) is incorrect. Pointing to a named part requires students to map a word they hear onto a picture, which taps receptive vocabulary. The student produces no sentence and no idea of their own.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A third-grade teacher wants students to understand how suffixes change the way a word works in a sentence. Which activity best targets that goal?
choices: Having students read multisyllabic words by dividing them into syllables
Having students look up base words in a dictionary and record the definitions
Having students practice reading words with the suffix -ed, focusing on its three pronunciations
Having students sort words ending in -ness, -ful, and -less according to the part of speech each suffix creates
items.correct_answer: Having students sort words ending in -ness, -ful, and -less according to the part of speech each suffix creates
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of morphological instruction. Sorting by the part of speech a suffix produces makes the grammatical work that suffixes do visible: -ness forms a noun, while -ful and -less form adjectives. Students see that changing the ending relocates the word within a sentence.

distractor_explanations.Having students read multisyllabic words: Substituting syllabication, which serves pronunciation, for morphological analysis, which serves meaning Dividing into syllables is a decoding procedure aimed at pronunciation. It directs attention to vowel patterns rather than to the meaningful units inside the word, so it does not address how suffixes change function.
distractor_explanations.Having students look up base words in a: Treating dictionary definition work as instruction in word structure Recording definitions treats each word as an isolated item to be looked up. It never asks students to compare base and affix, which is where the insight about how suffixes operate comes from.
distractor_explanations.Having students practice reading words w: Equating work on a suffix's pronunciation with work on its grammatical function The three pronunciations of -ed are a real decoding concern, but the activity targets sound, not function. Practicing pronunciation leaves untouched the question of what the suffix does to the word's role in a sentence.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Before his fifth-grade class reads a science article containing "photosynthesis," "chlorophyll," and "chloroplast," Mr. Osei wants to use those words to build vocabulary through direct instruction. Which move best integrates word analysis with that goal?
choices: Having students read the article independently and infer each term's meaning from context as they go
Teaching what photo-, chlor-, and -phyll mean, then guiding students to split the words into parts and check their meanings against the text
Giving students the definitions to copy before reading so that no instructional time is lost later
Asking each student to look up one word in the dictionary and write a sentence using it
items.correct_answer: Teaching what photo-, chlor-, and -phyll mean, then guiding students to split the words into parts and check their meanings against the text
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how word analysis carries direct vocabulary instruction. Teaching the recurring Greek elements and then having students take the words apart gives them a reusable key, since photo- and chlor- reappear in "photograph" and "chlorine." Checking the parts against the text ties the analysis to meaning instead of leaving it as a puzzle.

distractor_explanations.Having students read the article indepen: Assuming vocabulary is acquired incidentally through wide reading and context, without direct instruction Context in a dense science article rarely supplies enough information to fix a precise technical meaning, and students left to infer often settle on a vague or wrong sense. Incidental learning from context is slow and uneven; these words are worth teaching directly.
distractor_explanations.Giving students the definitions to copy: Equating handing students definitions with direct vocabulary instruction, skipping the active processing of word parts Handing over definitions is efficient but shallow: students receive words they have no way to unpack, so the knowledge does not extend to new words. Direct vocabulary instruction requires active processing of word parts and multiple meaningful encounters.
distractor_explanations.Asking each student to look up one word: Treating dictionary lookup as vocabulary teaching, since copying isolated definitions builds no analytical skill Dictionary definitions for technical terms are often harder than the words themselves, and copying one produces no analysis. The value of this word set lies in its shared parts, which a dictionary lookup leaves invisible.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Ms. Alvarez is preparing an onset-rime lesson for her kindergarten class. Several students are English learners who are still building oral vocabulary in English. Which modification to the lesson materials would best support those students?
choices: Removing the pictures and working with spoken words only, so that students attend to sounds rather than images
Pairing each spoken word with a picture whose name is already familiar, so students can manipulate the sounds of a word they know
Replacing the spoken words with printed word cards so students can see the shared rime
Adding a written sorting worksheet for students to complete on their own after the lesson
items.correct_answer: Pairing each spoken word with a picture whose name is already familiar, so students can manipulate the sounds of a word they know
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to modify examples and materials for particular learners. Onset-rime work is an oral task, and these students may not yet have a stable label for the word being taken apart. Pictures with familiar referents carry the vocabulary load, so the students' attention stays on the sound structure instead of on guessing what the word means.

distractor_explanations.Removing the pictures and working with s: Removing visual vocabulary supports on the assumption that images distract from auditory processing Option (A) is incorrect. Taking pictures away raises the language demand precisely for the students who need it lowered. A child who is unsure what the word means cannot manipulate its parts, so the task would end up measuring vocabulary rather than phonological awareness.
distractor_explanations.Replacing the spoken words with printed: Converting an oral phonological task into a print-based decoding task Option (C) is incorrect. Putting the words in print shifts the task toward orthography and decoding. Onset-rime manipulation is meant to be done with the ear, and requiring print adds a demand these students are not ready for.
distractor_explanations.Adding a written sorting worksheet for s: Substituting an independent written worksheet for oral modeling and guided practice Option (D) is incorrect. An independent written sort removes both the oral response and the teacher's modeling, so students lose the feedback that tells them whether they split the word in the right place.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Two English learners in a second-grade class score below benchmark on a pseudoword decoding measure but perform at grade level on a listening comprehension task. Which conclusion is best supported by these results?
choices: The students have a language-based comprehension problem that calls for intensive vocabulary instruction
The students' difficulty is at the level of word recognition, so decoding instruction is warranted and listening comprehension is a strength to build on
The screening is not valid for English learners and the results should be set aside
The students should be referred for special education evaluation before any instruction is changed
items.correct_answer: The students' difficulty is at the level of word recognition, so decoding instruction is warranted and listening comprehension is a strength to build on
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how assessment data are interpreted for diverse learners. Pseudoword decoding draws little on English oral vocabulary, so a low score points to word recognition, while grade-level listening comprehension shows that language comprehension is developing normally. Together the two results locate the difficulty precisely and indicate that decoding instruction, not vocabulary intervention, is the next step.

distractor_explanations.The students have a language-based compr: Reading the assessment results backwards, since grade-level listening comprehension rules out a language-comprehension problem The listening comprehension data contradict this reading: the students understand language at grade level. Intensive vocabulary instruction would target the one area in which they are performing well.
distractor_explanations.The screening is not valid for English l: Assuming standardized screeners are invalid for English learners and discarding data that are in fact interpretable Because pseudowords carry no meaning, the measure does not penalize a smaller English vocabulary the way a passage reading task can. Setting aside valid information would leave a real decoding difficulty unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.The students should be referred for spec: Assuming a low screening score requires a special education referral before instruction is adjusted and the response monitored Screening data are meant to inform instruction first. A structured response of targeted decoding instruction with progress monitoring is the appropriate next step, and referral enters the picture only if students fail to respond.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Screening shows that most of Ms. Adeyemi's kindergarten class can produce rhymes and blend onsets and rimes, but only three students can segment the three phonemes in a word such as ship. Which response best reflects systematic and explicit instruction?
choices: Keeping the class moving through onset-rime work while adding a daily small-group routine that models phoneme segmentation, guides practice with counters, and reviews sounds already taught
Returning the whole class to rhyming and syllable work until every student has reached mastery of those levels
Waiting to address phonemes until students begin reading, since phonemic awareness develops as a result of reading print
Providing phoneme instruction only in one-on-one tutoring sessions and leaving it out of whole-class time
items.correct_answer: Keeping the class moving through onset-rime work while adding a daily small-group routine that models phoneme segmentation, guides practice with counters, and reviews sounds already taught
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how systematic and explicit instruction responds to assessment data. Systematic instruction follows a planned sequence, so the class continues at the onset-rime level while a small group gets the additional, more demanding work those three students need. Explicit instruction supplies the modeling, guided practice, and cumulative review that make the harder level learnable rather than assumed.

distractor_explanations.Returning the whole class to rhyming and: Reads holding the whole class until everyone masters a level as the careful choice, when systematic teaching advances on sequence and answers individual gaps in small groups. Holding the entire class at a level most students have already mastered postpones instruction the class is ready for, and it still does not give the three students what they are missing at the phoneme level.
distractor_explanations.Waiting to address phonemes until studen: Inverts the causal direction, assuming that reading print will hand students phonemic awareness rather than drawing on it as the foundation decoding requires. The causal direction runs the other way. Phonemic awareness supports learning to read, so waiting for reading to produce it inverts the relationship and leaves students without the foundation decoding requires.
distractor_explanations.Providing phoneme instruction only in on: Treats tiered support as a stand-in for core instruction instead of an addition layered on top of strong whole-class teaching. Tiered support adds to core instruction; it does not replace it. Removing phoneme work from the whole-class block leaves the class dependent on pull-out time that is usually too short to close the gap.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: During an informal assessment, a teacher asks a first grader to blend the sounds /d/ /o/ /g/. The student responds "d... o... g... doh." Which statement best describes the student's difficulty?
choices: The student cannot blend individual phonemes into a word, an undeveloped phonemic awareness skill
The student has acquired the alphabetic principle but lacks sight word recognition
The student has a speech sound production disorder that interferes with decoding
The student reads with insufficient fluency to support comprehension
items.correct_answer: The student cannot blend individual phonemes into a word, an undeveloped phonemic awareness skill
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to interpret informal assessment data. The student produces the phonemes in sequence but cannot fuse them into a word, which indicates a gap in blending, a foundational phonemic awareness skill that must precede successful decoding.

distractor_explanations.The student has acquired the alphabetic: Assuming that because a student can produce letter sounds, the alphabetic principle is in place. Producing sounds and blending them into a word are distinct achievements. Blending is precisely what the alphabetic principle requires. If the student could map letters to sounds and then fuse those sounds, the word would be read. Sight word recognition is a separate issue and is not what this response shows.
distractor_explanations.The student has a speech sound productio: Attributing a cognitive-linguistic gap to a speech or motor difficulty. Clear articulation in the response is the evidence that rules this out. The student articulated /d/, /o/, and /g/ clearly, which rules out a production problem. The breakdown is not in saying the sounds but in mentally combining them.
distractor_explanations.The student reads with insufficient flue: Applying a broad label such as fluency to any observed reading difficulty, which obscures the specific skill that needs teaching. Fluency concerns reading connected text with accuracy, rate, and prosody. This student has not yet blended a single spoken word, so the difficulty lies at a more basic level than fluency.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A fourth-grade student reads the word "unhappy" accurately. When asked what it means, the student says, "It means you are happy again — the 'un' part makes it happen two times." Which analysis of this response is most accurate?
choices: The student has confused the prefix un- with the prefix re-.
The student has correctly identified the base word but has not yet learned any prefixes.
The student has applied a closed-syllable decoding strategy to a multisyllabic word.
The student has confused the suffix -y with the prefix un-.
items.correct_answer: The student has confused the prefix un- with the prefix re-.
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to analyze student responses to identify partial conceptions. The student correctly identifies "happy" as the base and correctly recognizes that the added letters form an affix, but assigns the wrong meaning to it. The meaning given, "happen two times" or "again," is the meaning of re-, not un-. This is a partial conception: the structural analysis is sound while the semantic assignment is not.

distractor_explanations.The student has correctly identified the: Mistaking a partial conception for the complete absence of one. Because the structural analysis is sound, instruction should refine the idea rather than start over. This analysis understates what the student demonstrated. The student did apply prefix knowledge by attributing a specific meaning to un-, which means instruction should refine an existing concept rather than introduce prefixes from scratch.
distractor_explanations.The student has applied a closed-syllabl: Confusing a decoding difficulty with a meaning difficulty. Accurate oral reading rules out syllabication as the obstacle and points to morphological meaning instead. The student read the word accurately, so decoding is not the difficulty. The error appears only when the student explains the meaning, which places the problem at the level of morphological meaning rather than syllable-based word attack.
distractor_explanations.The student has confused the suffix -y w: Misjudging where the affix boundary falls by taking a letter inside the base as the affix under discussion. The student's explicit reference to un- is the decisive evidence. The student's comment focuses entirely on "un" and attributes a meaning to it. The final -y in "happy" belongs to the base word and plays no part in the student's explanation, so the confusion is between two prefixes, not between a prefix and a suffix.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: During a science discussion, a fifth-grade student says, 'The water evaporated, so it disappeared and it is gone forever.' Which teacher response best targets the particular concept in need of attention?
choices: 'Can someone else give us a better sentence using evaporated?'
'That is a good try, but disappeared is the wrong word. Please say your sentence again using evaporated.'
'You are right that the water is no longer in the cup. Where did it go, and what form is it in now?'
'Let us look up evaporate in the dictionary, and then everyone can copy the definition.'
items.correct_answer: 'You are right that the water is no longer in the cup. Where did it go, and what form is it in now?'
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to respond to student talk so that the response targets the concept at issue. The student has used the target word correctly and has one part of the idea, that the water is no longer visible, but has attached the everyday meaning of disappearance to it. Asking where the water went and what form it is in now presses directly on the missing piece, that matter changes state rather than ceasing to exist, while building on what the student already has right.

distractor_explanations.'Can someone else give us a better sente: Equating hearing a better answer from a classmate with revising one's own thinking; the original speaker never examines their own reasoning Handing the question to another student bypasses the student who needs the help. The original speaker hears a better sentence without ever examining the assumption behind their own.
distractor_explanations.'That is a good try, but disappeared is: Mistaking a conceptual error for a word-choice error; a student can restate the term and still hold the original misunderstanding This response treats the difficulty as a word choice problem, but the student already used evaporated appropriately. Asking for the word again leaves the underlying idea, that the water still exists in another form, completely unaddressed.
distractor_explanations.'Let us look up evaporate in the diction: Assuming an authoritative definition corrects a misconception; a definition the student never reconciles with their own idea does not replace it A dictionary definition supplies authoritative wording, but copying it does not require the student to reconcile the definition with what they just said. A student can write the definition and continue to believe that the water is simply gone.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: During a unit on the water cycle, a fourth-grade teacher wants students to learn the domain-specific words "evaporation," "condensation," and "precipitation." Which plan best combines direct instruction with independent learning?
choices: Explaining each term with examples and non-examples, then having students independently build a word map with a student-friendly definition, a sketch, and one use of the word
Writing the terms on a chart and having students copy the definitions into their notebooks
Telling students to look up any words they do not know while they read the chapter
Posting a list of the terms and telling students they will be quizzed on Friday
items.correct_answer: Explaining each term with examples and non-examples, then having students independently build a word map with a student-friendly definition, a sketch, and one use of the word
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how direct instruction and independent learning work together to build vocabulary. The teacher's explanation with examples and non-examples establishes the boundaries of each concept, and the word map then requires each student to process the word again alone, linking a definition, an image, and a use. Domain-specific terms need both the teacher's framing and the student's own processing.

distractor_explanations.Writing the terms on a chart and having: Assuming exposure to a definition produces knowledge of a word Option (B) is incorrect. Copying definitions moves the words from one surface to another without requiring students to work out what they mean, so the terms remain unconnected to the concepts. This option reflects the common misconception that exposure to a definition produces knowledge of a word.
distractor_explanations.Telling students to look up any words th: Assuming domain-specific vocabulary is picked up incidentally through reading without direct teaching Option (C) is incorrect. Leaving students to look words up on their own assumes they will notice the unknown word, have a usable source, and process what they find, none of which can be counted on. This option reflects the common misconception that vocabulary is picked up incidentally through reading and needs no direct teaching.
distractor_explanations.Posting a list of the terms and telling: Assuming the prospect of a test can stand in for teaching word meanings Option (D) is incorrect. Announcing a quiz creates a reason to study but provides no instruction on what the words mean, leaving students to invent meanings or memorize strings of letters. This option reflects the common misconception that the prospect of a test can stand in for teaching.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Which statement best describes the primary purpose of preteaching key vocabulary before students read a content-area text?
choices: It reduces the number of unfamiliar words in the text so that attention is available for constructing meaning rather than for stopping at words
It ensures that students will be able to spell the academic terms correctly on the unit assessment
It gives students a written list of definitions to consult while they read
It allows the teacher to address the vocabulary standards before moving on to comprehension

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A third-grade student reads a grade-level passage aloud accurately and at an acceptable rate, but in a flat, word-by-word monotone with pauses that ignore punctuation. The student's comprehension is limited by oral language proficiency rather than by any aspect of reading
The student needs additional phonics instruction to decode multisyllabic words
items.correct_answer: The student reads accurately but without prosody, and the absence of phrasing limits the grouping of words into meaningful units that supports comprehension
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how fluency contributes to comprehension. Accuracy and rate are present, so the missing element is prosody: pausing at phrase boundaries and using stress and intonation to signal how words group. distractor_explanations.The student's comprehension is limited b: Attributing a comprehension difficulty to language background without evidence, which recasts a teachable fluency problem as a fixed language factor Nothing in the description identifies this student as an English learner, and oral language proficiency is only one of several possible sources of a comprehension difficulty. Attributing the problem to language background without evidence risks withholding instruction the student actually needs.
distractor_explanations.The student needs additional phonics ins: Attributing every reading difficulty to decoding; the student already read accurately, so phonics is not the needed next step The student read the passage accurately, which is direct evidence that decoding is working on this text. items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Ms. Alvarez's third graders stop at the sentence "The arid desert received almost no rain all year." She wants to show them how to work out the meaning of "arid" by combining context, syntax, and word-structure knowledge. Which teacher move best models that process?

Having the students skip the word, finish the sentence, and put in a word that sounds right
Telling the students that arid means "dry" and having them write the definition three times
Asking what the sentence says happens to the desert, what part of speech arid must be, and whether any word parts look familiar, then checking the candidate meaning against the sentence
items.correct_answer: Asking what the sentence says happens to the desert, what part of speech arid must be, and whether any word parts look familiar, then checking the candidate meaning against the sentence
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how systematic and explicit instruction is delivered for word-solving. By asking what the sentence reports, what part of speech the word must be, and whether any word parts are familiar, the teacher models a routine that draws on context, syntax, and morphology together and then verifies the candidate meaning against the sentence. The questioning makes the thinking visible, so students can run the same routine on the next unfamiliar word without her.

distractor_explanations.Having the students sound out arid sylla: Treating successful decoding as if it yielded meaning, when it yields only pronunciation. Option (C) is incorrect. Sounding out arid helps students pronounce the word, but pronunciation does not deliver meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that decoding a word and understanding it are a single achievement. Students who can read a word aloud accurately may still have no idea what it means.
distractor_explanations.Having the students skip the word, finis: Treating an unverified plausible substitution as equivalent to a checked inference from context and word structure. Option (D) is incorrect. Substituting a word that sounds right may produce a plausible reading, but plausibility is not evidence, and students have no way to tell whether their guess matches the author's meaning. This option reflects the common misconception that any context-based guess counts as strategic word learning. Without checking the guess against context, syntax, and word parts, the strategy is unreliable.
distractor_explanations.Telling the students that arid means \"d: Confusing the delivery of an answer with the teaching of a procedure, so that explicit instruction is reduced to telling. Option (A) is incorrect. Supplying the definition ends the reasoning before it begins and leaves students with nothing to use on the next unfamiliar word. This option reflects the common misconception that telling a word's meaning is teaching a strategy. A definition is a product; the transferable thing is the procedure for arriving at it.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: Before reading a short play, a fourth-grade teacher introduces the terms dialogue, scene, and stage directions with student-friendly definitions, several examples and non-examples, and a wall chart students will use while reading. Which evaluation of this approach is most accurate?

It gives students direct instruction in the labels they need to notice, discuss, and analyze the structural features that carry meaning in a play
It will work only if students memorize the definitions before reading, because knowing definitions is what determines comprehension
It removes the need to teach comprehension strategies, because once students know the terms they will understand the play
items.correct_answer: It gives students direct instruction in the labels they need to notice, discuss, and analyze the structural features that carry meaning in a play
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how direct vocabulary instruction supports comprehension of genre features. Terms such as scene and stage directions name the structures that carry a play's meaning: stage directions tell readers what a spectator would see, and scene boundaries signal shifts in time and place. Teaching these words directly with examples and non-examples gives students the language to talk about the structure, and explicit teaching of this kind is more efficient than leaving such low-frequency academic terms to incidental acquisition.

distractor_explanations.It is misguided, because vocabulary of t: Assuming all vocabulary is best acquired incidentally through wide reading; direct instruction is indicated for academic and text-structure terms. distractor_explanations.It removes the need to teach comprehensi: Treating vocabulary knowledge as a replacement for comprehension strategies; vocabulary supports meaning construction but does not substitute for it. Comprehension strategy instruction is still required.

Building a word with tiles forces the student to analyze the spoken word into phonemes and select a grapheme for each one; reading it back forces the reverse operation on the identical spelling. items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A fourth-grade teacher asks students to rewrite a scene from a story using the voice of a different character. Which understanding of literary devices does this activity best develop?

Setting establishes when and where events occur and can be changed without altering a character's motivation
Character development is shown mainly through physical description rather than through what a character thinks
Point of view determines which events and thoughts the reader has access to, so changing the narrator changes the meaning of the scene
items.correct_answer: Point of view determines which events and thoughts the reader has access to, so changing the narrator changes the meaning of the scene
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how point of view functions as a literary device. Because a narrator can report only what that character perceives, knows, and cares about, the same events told from another position will include different facts and carry different weight. Rewriting the scene forces students to discover this directly: the events stay put while the meaning shifts, which is exactly the point the activity is designed to teach.

A student could rewrite the scene from another character's perspective using plain literal language throughout, and the exercise would still work, which shows that imagery is not the operative device here.
distractor_explanations.Setting establishes when and where event: Relegates setting to inert backdrop, ignoring how strongly where and when events unfold constrains what a character can want or do. Setting is a structural element, but the activity does not relocate or redate the scene. More importantly, the claim that setting can be changed without affecting motivation is itself questionable, since where and when events occur routinely shapes what characters want and can do.
distractor_explanations.Character development is shown mainly th: Narrows character development to physical description, overlooking a character's thoughts, speech, and choices, the routes authors chiefly rely on to reveal character. Physical description is the least reliable route to character development, and the activity asks students to work with a character's voice and thoughts. Rewriting from another position requires attending to what that character notices and believes, which is internal rather than descriptive.

This option reflects the common misconception that frequent progress monitoring is a route to referral. A weekly retell used to decide on reteaching stays entirely inside the instructional cycle.
distractor_explanations.A standardized assessment that allows co: Treating uniform administration to the whole class as standardization, which also requires normed and comparable scoring Standardized assessment requires fixed administration, normed scoring, and evidence supporting comparison across groups; a teacher-made weekly retell has none of these. items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: After a small-group lesson on making inferences, Ms. Ortiz asks each student to write one sentence naming an inference they made and the sentence from the text that led to it. She reads the slips before forming the next day's groups. Which evaluation of this activity is most accurate?
choices: It is an informal formative assessment that makes students' thinking visible, so she can see whether they are grounding inferences in text evidence and regroup accordingly
It is an informal assessment, but it measures writing mechanics rather than comprehension, so it cannot guide reading instruction
It is a formal summative assessment because it produces a written product that can be scored
It is mainly a comprehension strategy lesson, and its usefulness ends once students have filled in the slip
items.correct_answer: It is an informal formative assessment that makes students' thinking visible, so she can see whether they are grounding inferences in text evidence and regroup accordingly
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how to evaluate instructional activities for the thinking they reveal. Asking for both the inference and the supporting sentence requires students to show their reasoning rather than only their answer, which lets the teacher distinguish a student who guessed from one who used evidence. Because the slips are read immediately and used to form the next day's groups, the activity functions formatively: it is ungraded, quick, and directly changes what happens next.

distractor_explanations.It is an informal assessment, but it mea: Judging an assessment by the format of the response instead of by the construct it samples; the response mode does not determine what is measured. Writing is the vehicle here, not the object. The teacher reads the slips for the relationship between claim and evidence, and a slip with weak mechanics can still show sound reasoning, or the reverse.
distractor_explanations.It is a formal summative assessment beca: Treating any written, scoreable product as formal and summative; the distinguishing feature is how the results are used, not their physical form. Formal summative assessment uses standardized administration and scoring to report achievement after instruction. This exit slip has no scoring rubric, is administered by the classroom teacher, and is used to adjust tomorrow's teaching, all of which make it informal and formative.
distractor_explanations.It is mainly a comprehension strategy le: Seeing an assessment encounter only as practice; the same activity can both develop thinking and yield data, and the data should drive instruction. The activity does give students practice, but the teacher collects and reads the slips for a reason. Overlooking the information they carry discards the evidence that should shape the next lesson.

items.subject: Teaching Reading
items.stem: A teacher wants to help students see that decoding and encoding are reciprocal skills. Which activity best demonstrates that connection?
choices: Having students practice spelling lists of words that follow the week's phonics pattern
Having students reread the same text three times to build fluency
Having students sort pictures by their initial sound
Having students read a decodable text and then write sentences using words from that text
items.correct_answer: Having students read a decodable text and then write sentences using words from that text
items.explanation: The question requires an understanding of how decoding and encoding reinforce one another. Reading words from the text and then writing those same words moves students in both directions over identical spellings, making the print-to-sound and sound-to-print routes practice each other.

distractor_explanations.Having students practice spelling lists: Treating one half of a reciprocal relationship as if it were the whole. Encoding practice alone does not demonstrate that the two processes support each other. Spelling words that follow a pattern exercises encoding, but with no reading component the connection is never made explicit. Students may spell the words correctly and still not link them to the words they read.
distractor_explanations.Having students reread the same text thr: Selecting a fluency routine for a task that requires linking reading to writing. Fluency practice works within one direction only. Rereading targets automaticity and prosody in oral reading. It involves no writing and therefore cannot show students anything about encoding.
distractor_explanations.Having students sort pictures by their i: Choosing an activity at the wrong level of the literacy hierarchy. The target connection requires both reading and writing of real words. Sorting pictures by initial sound is a phonemic awareness task. It sits below decoding and well below encoding, so it cannot illustrate a relationship between them.
